coreDualNarrative.present: Theo, Rae and Adrian discover that an erased war is bleeding back into reality and that the consequences of forgetting were never actually removed.
coreDualNarrative.past: The warrior-god ensemble gradually reveals, through complete dramatic memory-vignettes, what the forgotten war was, why it could not be won, and why Mero and Adrian chose the Reset.
coreDualNarrative.collision: The two stories converge when Theo and Rae recover not only the war but their own participation in it, and the present recreates the moral choice that ended the ancient conflict.

formalEscalation: Issue 1: present-dominant with one intrusive memory rupture.
Issue 2: past-dominant with minimal present-day framing.
Issue 3: present-dominant; memory is shorter but materially consequential.
Issue 4: past-dominant; ends with Adrian revealing Theo and Rae were there.
Issue 5: roughly 50/50; prior memories are revisited and ancient Theo/Rae become visible inside them.
Issue 6: shorter intercuts; personal memory and replacement history begin contradicting one another.
Issue 7: alternating pages; the same moral problems occur in past and present in parallel.
Issue 8: convergence; pages and eventually panels cease obeying a stable past/present boundary.
warriorRevealRule: Exactly one previously unseen warrior god/champion is fully introduced per issue. Previously introduced champions may recur. Names, symbols, titles or indirect references to later champions are permitted before visual/dramatic introduction.

reservedForLater.Regent: Named and historically real but not fully revealed in the first eight issues. Regent remains the unrevealed champion whose stability/rigidity philosophy can deepen later arcs rather than overcrowd season one.
reservedForLater.GeneralMero: Not counted against the one-warrior-god-per-issue cadence because Mero is explicitly human: a general walking among gods. He can appear in ancient vignettes before Theo's ancient self is revealed.
reservedForLater.AncientAdrian: Do not clearly show Adrian's ancient role before the midpoint. His historical presence should become legible only when the identity structure is revealed.

issues.title: THE WEIGHT OF DEAD IRON
issues.presentStory: At Olyria-Prime, Theo finds the Desert Marker exactly where impossible dreams told him it would be. Rae separately sees an erased place and a forbidden Redlin reference reappear in the Zenith archive. Adrian recognizes what has started and tries to contain knowledge rather than explain it.
issues.memoryVignette: Theo touches the Marker and the present is replaced by the last quiet moment before a catastrophic battle. Starbreaker stands over a collapsing star or stellar weapon in suspended anticipation. The memory ends before detonation. No ancient Theo is visible. Redlin may be named or indicated as the opposing force but is not yet shown as a person.
issues.historicalTruth: The impossible images are not fantasies: the Desert Marker was part of a real war, and Starbreaker was a real participant.
issues.readerMisunderstanding: Theo and the reader still believe he is receiving someone else's history. Starbreaker can still be mistaken for an uncomplicated hero.
issues.presentConsequence: The Marker and archive react because meaning is returning. Theo keeps a physical fragment; Rae preserves a forbidden name; Adrian knows both are dangerous.
issues.endTurn: Theo forces Adrian to admit that he also remembers the impossible sky, but Adrian refuses to say whose memory it is.

issues.title: GLASS DUST AND VIOLET LIGHT
issues.presentStory: Brief present-day bookends: Theo and Rae discover that they remember incompatible versions of the same battle; Adrian refuses to adjudicate which one is true.
issues.memoryVignette: A full dramatic chapter from the Desert Marker conflict. Starbreaker presses for a decisive strike; Redlin tries to contain escalation before it propagates beyond the battlefield. Mero is present as the human commander trying to hold a coalition together. The scene should contain history, familiarity and old grievance: Starbreaker and Redlin know each other well enough to predict the other's argument. The detonation is still withheld or only partially witnessed.
issues.historicalTruth: The war was not heroes versus monsters. Starbreaker and Redlin were opposing people with coherent moral reasons and a history with each other.
issues.readerMisunderstanding: The reader assumes Theo's and Rae's contradictory memories come from different historical sources or inherited viewpoints, not from their own lives.
issues.presentConsequence: Theo begins idealizing Starbreaker's decisiveness; Rae sees Redlin's containment as a response to consequences Theo's memory omits.
issues.endTurn: Theo and Rae can describe private details from the same scene that no surviving record contains. Adrian recognizes the significance but still withholds the identity truth.

issues.title: THE ARCHITECTURE OF RUIN
issues.presentStory: At Vael-Tor, dormant defenses and a buried dreadnought reassert themselves around current civilian life. A refugee crisis forces Rae and Theo to choose present people over the apparent logic of ancient defenses. Adrian finally admits that forgetting did not erase physical matter.
issues.memoryVignette: A shorter vision of Atlas physically holding a world together while Starbreaker argues that preserving it will prolong or widen the war. Atlas refuses to make civilians into an acceptable loss. No ancient Theo or Rae is shown.
issues.historicalTruth: The war's consequences were embedded in worlds, architecture and populations; the Reset removed meaning, not matter. Atlas demonstrates that the ancient conflict already contained disputes over who was being protected and at what cost.
issues.readerMisunderstanding: Atlas appears morally clearer than Starbreaker because the memory shows protection without yet showing the downstream cost of refusing sacrifice.
issues.presentConsequence: The buried dreadnought surfaces. Present institutions must confront an object too large to dismiss as hallucination or archive error.
issues.endTurn: Adrian states the essential rule plainly: history was forgotten; the thing itself was never gone.

issues.title: SILENCE IN THE VAULT
issues.presentStory: Theo, Rae and Adrian reach Pax-Aeterna, a site remembered as an empty treaty vault. Their presence causes a much larger historical sequence to return.
issues.memoryVignette: A failed negotiation and civilization-scale triage crisis. Arbiter must decide whether a threatened system can be allowed to survive when both factions believe its continuation may widen the war. Atlas refuses sacrificial logic; Redlin argues containment; Starbreaker argues the danger cannot be left unresolved; Mero tries to preserve a path that does not exist. Arbiter eventually authorizes an extinction-level act. The scene is not a courtroom abstraction: each character has something personal at stake and someone will live with the decision afterward.
issues.historicalTruth: Both sides crossed moral lines. The war's horror came from valid principles becoming catastrophic when applied at universal scale.
issues.readerMisunderstanding: Theo and Rae still think they are witnessing recovered history. Their emotional reactions feel excessive but remain unexplained.
issues.midpointReveal: After the memory, Theo and Rae separately recall small details that were never visible in the recovered scene. Adrian finally says the truth: they were not shown this history. They were there. He reveals that Theo served Mero and Rae served Arbiter, but does not yet tell them what either of them personally did.
issues.endTurn: The question changes from 'whose memories are these?' to 'what did I do there?'

issues.title: EMBERS OF THE ZENITH
issues.presentStory: Theo and Rae resist Adrian's claim, then deliberately return to places and objects that triggered the earliest memories. Their current identities begin destabilizing as autobiographical continuity returns.
memoryVignettes: Revisit Issue 1's Starbreaker scene. The composition widens and ancient Theo is finally visible behind Mero as a junior attaché. Mero addresses him casually, proving that the memory once had an 'I' inside it.
Revisit Issue 4's Arbiter sequence. Rae is visible beside Arbiter recording the ruling. The remembered scene continues beyond the original ending and shows Rae reacting privately to the decision.

New vignette: Afterlight moves through the aftermath trying to restore a devastated civilization. Starbreaker expects recovery to validate decisive destruction; Afterlight tells him the war is destroying life faster than she can restore it. Their relationship should carry exhaustion and prior affection or respect, not merely ideological labels.
issues.historicalTruth: Theo and Rae were not passive witnesses. They occupied real roles inside the institutions making these decisions. Restoration has limits; not everything the war destroyed could be recovered even before the Reset.
issues.readerMisunderstanding: Theo and Rae still hope their ancient roles were clerical proximity rather than moral participation.
issues.presentConsequence: Personal objects, handwriting and habits begin returning with context. Their present histories remain coherent, but no longer feel complete.
issues.endTurn: Rae remembers the beginning of a sentence she once said to Arbiter but not how she finished it. Theo remembers Mero asking him for an opinion. Both realize their own choices are still missing.

issues.title: THE MARGIN OF ERROR
issues.presentStory: Theo and Rae test Adrian's claim against the world itself and discover that the supposedly vast gulf between the war and the present behaves like scar tissue: personal artifacts, places and records fit their memories too directly to belong to remote antiquity. Adrian admits the Reset created continuity without restoring truth.
issues.memoryVignette: Flux is shown as a person living with unbearable uncertainty, not as a probability machine. Flux refuses demands for certainty from allies who want a prediction that will justify action. Mero asks for guidance; Flux can only describe futures in which every faction becomes what it fears. Later in the issue Flux disappears before the Reset. The disappearance is not explained and remains a genuine hole even in Adrian's memory.
issues.historicalTruth: The apparent age of the forgotten war cannot be trusted. Reality healed around a missing continuity. The ancient record itself also contains real absences that the Reset did not create, including Flux's disappearance.
issues.readerMisunderstanding: The characters are tempted to believe Adrian understands the full structure of the scar; Flux's disappearance proves he does not.
issues.presentConsequence: Theo and Rae begin remembering their own spoken lines and choices in fragments. Modern people beyond them start experiencing small contradictory memories that do not fit official history.
issues.endTurn: Someone with no known connection to the war recognizes a place, relationship or loss from the erased history. The return is no longer confined to Theo and Rae.

issues.title: GRAVITY AND CONSEQUENCE
issues.presentStory: Replacement history begins failing in public. At a modern city built over Neo-Vectra, people remember incompatible loyalties, relationships and losses. Theo, Rae and Adrian try to keep the present from turning those memories immediately into renewed factions.
issues.memoryVignette: Alternating pages reconstruct the ancient Neo-Vectra crisis. Oryon sees catastrophe coming and argues that waiting is itself a choice that will kill worlds. Atlas resists sacrificing civilians; Arbiter weighs triage; Starbreaker wants decisive action; Redlin fears escalation; Mero discovers that every available solution reproduces the logic of the war. Flux's absence hangs over the debate. Theo and Rae now appear naturally in the past pages because the midpoint secret is gone.
issues.historicalTruth: The war became unwinnable because every side's attempt to prevent catastrophe generated the conditions for another catastrophe. Oryon's control grows from anticipatory grief rather than villainy.
issues.personalReveal: Theo remembers giving Mero advice that helped move the coalition toward the final decision. Rae remembers participating in Arbiter's triage framework. Neither can retreat to 'I only watched.'
issues.presentConsequence: Present-day people begin acting on recovered ancient loyalties. Reality's remembered history threatens to become behavior, not merely recollection.
issues.endTurn: Adrian admits what full return may mean: not simply truth restored, but billions of people recovering lives, loves, hatreds and obligations that contradict the lives they believe they have lived.

issues.title: THE SHAPE OF TOMORROW
issues.presentStory: The scar of the Reset opens widely enough that past and present cease behaving as separate narrative spaces. Theo, Rae and Adrian reach the place where the Reset was enacted while the ancient decision returns around them.
issues.memoryVignette: Kyn enters the final ancient debate as the empath who can feel suffering at civilization scale. Oryon argues that catastrophe must be prevented; Arbiter insists someone must own the impossible choice; Kyn makes the case that continued memory of the war itself is perpetuating suffering; Mero realizes victory is impossible. Adrian, still an envoy rather than a ruler, is asked to carry out the act precisely because he has moved between every side. Mero authorizes the Reset. Ancient Theo and Rae are present and their own final positions are revealed.
issues.historicalTruth: The Reset was neither a secret superweapon nor a technical solution. It was a morally catastrophic act of imposed forgetting chosen because the war's participants could no longer imagine a way to stop reproducing the conflict.
issues.presentDilemma: Adrian wants to repeat the Reset. Theo, horrified by stolen history, is tempted to force complete restoration. Rae recognizes both as the same error: deciding for everyone what they are allowed to remember.
issues.resolution: They refuse both universal forgetting and forced universal restoration. They relinquish control over memory itself and allow reality to return continuity unevenly, person by person and place by place. The choice does not make the consequences safe; it refuses to solve moral conflict through coercion again.
issues.formalPayoff: Past and present compositions merge. Modern actions rhyme with ancient actions until the reader can follow continuity without labels. The climax should resolve through repeated moral choice, not through explaining a mechanism.
issues.finalImage: After the immediate crisis settles, a region of the night sky is simply wrong: familiar stars are absent. No one can explain whether they were erased, never existed in the replacement history, or have been lost by the returning one. Reality remembering has consequences beyond memory.
issues.openDoor: Regent remains unrevealed as a major ancient figure associated with stability. Flux remains missing. The universe has begun remembering, but nobody knows what complete continuity will restore.
